steps.lookCheck: Have the palette available for preparation, then choose a few familiar notes. Memorizing every fret is not required.
steps.listenCheck: Hear A7 at the beginning and know D7 arrives at bar 5.

steps.title: Set the four-bar boundary
steps.action: Count the lead-in or one full chorus, then enter at bar 1. Let the accompaniment continue while you create a question and answer through bars 1–4.
steps.lookCheck: The performance window is four complete bars. Keep a private count even if the phrase starts after beat 1.
steps.listenCheck: Rests are intentional time inside the phrase; the underlying music does not pause.

steps.title: Use the palette deliberately
steps.action: Choose from A, C, D, E, G. Repeat or vary an idea rather than racing through positions. If a wrong fret sounds, keep time and note the mistake afterward.
steps.lookCheck: Avoid new bends for this check; fretted notes make your intended pitch choices easier to identify.
steps.listenCheck: A is a useful landing note. The C against A7 is an intentional blues colour; an accidental outside note is a pitch-choice error to review.

steps.title: Finish and report separately
steps.action: Finish the four-bar phrase as D7 begins at bar 5, then stop your lead line while accompaniment continues. Report continuity, note choices and accompaniment alignment as separate observations.
steps.lookCheck: A take with a restart or lost bar cannot become continuous because its ending was good. An accidental outside note is not erased by a later correct note.
steps.listenCheck: Hear whether your final phrase landed within the intended window, rather than one beat after the form moved on.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I stop the whole pulse to find a note.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Reduce the note set to A and C and practise four counted bars with rests. Repeat the full check with accompaniment when the pulse holds.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I stay in the note set but lose the bar number.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Rehearse entering on bar 1 and finishing at bar 5 with one repeated A before adding improvisation.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I have only a metronome available.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Practise the full phrase and label it click-only preparation. Return to the over-form check when known accompaniment or a partner is available.

practiceSegments.instruction: Confirm accompaniment, key, tempo and chorus entry.
Warm up a small palette and rehearse the four-bar boundary.
Play a new four-bar phrase with the accompaniment continuing.
Review continuity, note choices and alignment independently.
Repair one issue and state whether the actual checkpoint conditions were met.

criteria: Known A-blues accompaniment continued throughout my four bars.
I followed bars 1–4 without a restart or lost bar, including intentional rests.
My intended and sounded notes stayed in A, C, D, E, G.
I finished at the boundary leading into bar 5.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Your own review confirms one continuous four-bar improvisation in the taught blues palette and in the correct accompaniment window.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Rehearse the first failing dimension: palette, pulse or form alignment. Keep click-only and interrupted practice distinct from this complete target.
selfAssessment.proves: Learner-reported four-bar improvisation with the stated accompaniment conditions.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Automatic key detection, microphone-certified continuity, artistic quality, unfamiliar-key fluency or an included backing track.

lessons.title: Pitch You Control After the Pick
lessons.sourceTitle: Pitch You Control After the Pick
lessons.objective: Distinguish a bend that reaches a new pitch from controlled vibrato, and prepare a comfortable semitone bend from F#4 to G4.

steps.title: Learn the two pitches before bending
steps.action: On string 2, play fret 7, then fret 8 normally: F#4 then G4. One fret is one semitone. Use the separate synthesized reference cells if needed, then stop them before your own notes.
steps.lookCheck: The target is a pitch interval, not a fixed sideways travel distance or a turn of the tuning peg.
steps.listenCheck: Remember G4 clearly enough to compare it with a bend from F#4.

steps.title: Support a small bend
steps.action: Place ring finger on string 2 fret 7, with middle and index behind it on the same string around frets 6 and 5. Find comfortable thumb support. Pick once, then use a small coordinated hand rotation to move the string toward the thicker strings.
steps.lookCheck: The ring fingertip stays at fret 7; the hand supports it rather than extending one isolated finger. Stop if the movement hurts or the string resists beyond a comfortable attempt.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for pitch rising smoothly. Do not scrape into a new fretted note or add a second pick to disguise the bend.

steps.title: Reach, hold, mute, release
steps.action: Aim for the remembered G4, hold briefly, then mute with the picking hand before returning the string. Check the unbent fret-8 target again.
steps.lookCheck: Keep other strings quiet with available hand contact; do not hook an adjacent string under a fingernail.
steps.listenCheck: A pitch near the target is different from noise or another string ringing. The muted release should not add an unintended descending note.

steps.title: Contrast a small vibrato
steps.action: On a comfortable sustained fret-7 note, make small, even pitch rises and returns without changing fret. Use a slower, narrower motion first; stop after a few cycles and release the hand.
steps.lookCheck: This is fretting-hand vibrato, not a tremolo-arm exercise. Keep the movement controlled rather than shaking the instrument.
steps.listenCheck: Hear a regular pulse around the intended note area. A single rise held at G is a bend; repeated small rises and returns create this vibrato effect.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I push farther but cannot hear a clear pitch.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Stop, check the fretted starting note and mute other strings. Rebuild a smaller supported movement.

mistakeRecovery.observation: My pitch rises when I wanted a steady note.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Reduce vibrato width and speed. Hold the unbent note briefly before starting the first small movement.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The string catches or my finger hurts.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Mute and release. Check hand support and string contact before another attempt; do not force the semitone during this session.

practiceSegments.instruction: Play and remember the F#4 and G4 reference pitches.
Explore short, supported semitone bends with rests.
Practise reaching, holding, muting and releasing.
Compare a steady bend with narrow repeated vibrato movements.
Name the difference and your next comfort or pitch repair.

criteria: I can identify the starting pitch and semitone target.
I understand that the finger remains at fret 7 during the bend.
I can distinguish a held bend from a few controlled vibrato cycles.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Explain the difference and make a short comfortable movement that raises pitch, with a controlled stop. Numeric accuracy is assessed separately.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Use the two normally fretted reference notes and shorter movements; do not force a painful bend.
selfAssessment.proves: Self-checked technique distinction and initial pitch-control exploration.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: A measured ±20-cent bend, vibrato quality certification, safe setup certification or automatic technique detection.

lessons.title: Bend to Target
lessons.objective: Practise matching F#4-to-G4 semitone bends using a chromatic meter when available, then repeat by ear without live visual correction.

steps.title: Choose an appropriate pitch reference
steps.action: Tune normally, then use your own chromatic tuner or pitch meter showing G4 and cents at A4 = 440 Hz. First check string 2 fret 8 without a bend. GuitarHub’s standard-string tuner compares against open strings, so it is not the target meter for this exercise.
steps.lookCheck: Confirm both note and octave. A display saying G3 is not the G4 target.
steps.listenCheck: Hear the normally fretted G4; stop any reference playback before observing your guitar.

steps.title: Match with visual help
steps.action: From F#4 at fret 7, pick once and bend toward the thicker strings. Watch the external meter as a guide, approach G4, and hold briefly without vibrato. Mute, release and rest.
steps.lookCheck: Do not slide to fret 8, retune the string or count a momentary sweep through the target as a held pitch.
steps.listenCheck: Listen to the same rise you see. The sound should settle, not keep climbing while the display briefly flashes G.

steps.title: Reduce the visual help
steps.action: Play the normal fret-8 reference, look away, and make another bend. Decide by ear whether you reached it; then check the held pitch if still stable. Any adjustment made after looking is a guided correction, not a blind first result.
steps.lookCheck: Keep ear-led and visually corrected attempts separate. This lesson does not save a bend trace or cents values.
steps.listenCheck: Compare your original judgment with the meter, rather than replacing the memory of an inaccurate bend with its correction.

steps.title: Use an ear-only route honestly
steps.action: If a suitable meter is unavailable, alternate the normally fretted G4 with a bend from F#4 and listen for a match. This is useful practice; do not assign a numeric cents result by ear.
steps.lookCheck: Keep the same target and comfortable movement. The per-note reference buttons are not live pitch feedback.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for undershoot, overshoot and instability as qualitative observations.

steps.title: Rest and name the pattern
steps.action: Review several short attempts, not a continuous grip. State whether you tend to undershoot, overshoot or wobble, and whether your evidence came from a meter or your ears.
steps.lookCheck: A stable target hold has no added vibrato. Stop the session if discomfort persists.
steps.listenCheck: Make the next correction smaller and deliberate rather than increasing force on every attempt.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The display jumps between unrelated notes.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Mute neighbouring strings, let the pick transient settle and try a clean single note. No usable reading means no numeric conclusion.

mistakeRecovery.observation: Every bend overshoots before I correct it.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Approach more gradually and compare a smaller motion with the normally fretted reference. Keep the initial overshoot distinct from the final correction.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I watch a standard-open-string target and chase its centre.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Use a chromatic meter configured for G4. The centre of a different open-string target is not this bend’s target.

practiceSegments.instruction: Confirm the external meter, note, octave and reference pitch, or choose ear-only practice.
Make short visually guided bends with releases and rests.
Repeat by ear, then inspect any still-stable held pitch.
Repair the most common direction or stability error.
State the observation method and remaining uncertainty.

criteria: I know whether my feedback came from a suitable G4 meter or my ears.
I can separate an initial bend from a visually corrected one.
I can identify the most common pitch or stability error.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Make repeatable comfortable attempts and describe their observed direction and stability. Keep numeric claims only when an appropriate meter supplied them.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Return to the two normally fretted reference notes, reduce the movement and test isolated single-string input.
selfAssessment.proves: Self-reported bend practice with stated external or ear-only feedback.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Built-in arbitrary-target display, stored bend traces, a blind three-of-four result or inferred cents accuracy from listening alone.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: Semitone Within Twenty Cents
lessons.objective: Attempt four independent semitone bends with live feedback hidden and report whether at least three hold G4 within twenty cents, using actual external observations.

steps.title: Establish the measurement before the set
steps.action: Use a chromatic meter for G4 at A4 = 440 Hz, and verify string 2 fret 8 as the unbent target. Arrange a helper to observe the meter or your own external tuner recording for later review. Without usable hidden-feedback observations, this remains an unverified ear exercise.
steps.lookCheck: The four numbered attempts are selected before starting. The target is F#4 at fret 7 bent up to G4; do not change string or target within the set.
steps.listenCheck: Play the reference once, let it end, and remember its pitch.

steps.title: Make one blind attempt
steps.action: Look away before picking fret 7. Bend toward the remembered G4 and hold for one second without vibrato or another pick. Mute before returning the string. Do not watch and correct the pitch during this attempt.
steps.lookCheck: An observer or later recording checks the held portion; a flash through the correct range is not a stable hold.
steps.listenCheck: Hear one picked note rise and settle, with other strings quiet.

steps.title: Keep all four observations
steps.action: Rest and repeat until you have four attempts in the set. Record whether each held G4 between −20 and +20 cents for the one-second hold. Keep misses and unknown readings; do not replace them with later successes.
steps.lookCheck: A no-reading attempt is unknown, not a pass. An incompletely observed set cannot establish the numeric target.
steps.listenCheck: A sharp, flat or unstable result is useful information, even if a later corrected practice bend sounds good.

steps.title: Apply the stated rule
steps.action: Review after the set. At least three successful, fully observed attempts out of those four meet the target. Fewer successes, live visual steering, or missing observations leave the checkpoint unmet or unverified.
steps.lookCheck: This is externally observed and learner-reported evidence. GuitarHub does not verify, record or grade these cents in this lesson.
steps.listenCheck: Listen to the stable hold when reviewing; do not judge only the highest pitch reached.

steps.title: Use the result to plan a repair
steps.action: If the target was not established, name overshoot, undershoot, instability or measurement failure and return to the matching practice step. If it was, repeat another day without carrying forward old successes.
steps.lookCheck: Each new set starts with four new numbered attempts; no averaging or best-of-many selection.
steps.listenCheck: Restore a relaxed hand before repeating. Accuracy does not justify forcing a painful bend.

mistakeRecovery.observation: Three bends felt right but I have no meter observations.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Report ear-only practice. A twenty-cent threshold cannot be verified from that feeling alone.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I see G briefly while the pitch continues rising.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Treat the attempt as unstable. Practise stopping and holding the movement, then start a new set.

mistakeRecovery.observation: One attempt has no clear reading.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Keep it unknown and label the set incomplete. Fix the input conditions before a fresh four-attempt set.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I corrected a flat bend while looking at the display.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Use it as guided practice; it is not a hidden-feedback success. Begin a new blind attempt only after resting.

practiceSegments.instruction: Verify the external measurement method and pre-number four attempts.
Warm up the reference and comfortable motion before the observed set.
Make four blind attempts with rests; retain every observation.
Review the four held-pitch results and apply the three-of-four rule.
State established, unmet or unverified, and choose the next repair.

criteria: All four attempts used the same F#4-to-G4 semitone target and hidden live feedback.
An external observer or usable recording checked each one-second held portion.
At least three of the four held G4 within −20 to +20 cents without vibrato or a second pick.
I kept failures and unknowns and did not splice successful attempts from different sets.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: A fully observed set contains at least three qualifying blind bends out of four. Preserve the external-method label; no in-app verification is implied.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Report the actual count or unknown status, return to guided pitch practice, and make a new complete set later.
selfAssessment.proves: Learner-reported results from the stated external hidden-feedback measurement procedure, when observations exist.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: In-app cents verification, automatic target hiding, saved pitch traces, guitar-technique certification or a numeric pass from ear-only practice.

lessons.title: Triads: Three Notes, Many Shapes
lessons.objective: Identify root, third and fifth in basic major/minor triads and recognize the same three note names inside larger open-chord shapes.

steps.title: Define the scope correctly
steps.action: A basic major or minor triad uses three distinct note names: root, third and fifth. The title is shorthand for these chords; power chords omit the third and seventh chords add another note, so not every chord literally has three distinct notes.
steps.lookCheck: Count note names, not fingers or sounding strings. Doubling a note in another octave does not create a new chord member.
steps.listenCheck: Compare the idea with G5 from the earlier lesson: two pitch classes are not a complete major or minor triad.

steps.title: Find C inside a familiar shape
steps.action: Pick the open C-major chord’s sounding strings separately: C, E, G, C, E. Name the repetitions, then use the small C triad on strings 3–1 at frets 5,5,3.
steps.lookCheck: The small shape contains C4, E4 and G4 exactly once. Exclude strings 6–4 when playing it.
steps.listenCheck: Both voicings use C, E and G, although their register and fullness differ.

steps.title: Keep identity when note order changes
steps.action: Play the F triad on strings 3–1 at 2,1,1, then G at 4,3,3. These put the third at the bottom: A–C–F and B–D–G.
steps.lookCheck: The lowest sounding note need not be the root. Use all three note names to identify the chord.
steps.listenCheck: Hear each note clearly before the strum; a muted third removes information about major/minor quality.

steps.title: Compare major and minor thirds
steps.action: Compare A major at 6,5,5 with A minor at 5,5,5 on strings 3–1. Only the note on string 3 changes, from C# to C, while E and A remain.
steps.lookCheck: Major A contains A,C#,E; minor A contains A,C,E. Do not lower every note or change the root.
steps.listenCheck: Hear the quality change caused by the third. The single index barre in Am must leave all three strings clear.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I call a six-string chord a six-note triad.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: List distinct note names and remove octave duplicates before counting chord members.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I name F as A because A is its lowest note here.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Name all three notes A,C,F, then locate the root F. An inversion changes order, not the chord’s identity.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The small chord sounds incomplete.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Pick strings 3,2,1 separately and clear the dead note before adding any bass strings.

practiceSegments.instruction: Separate note names, octave doublings and chord types.
Compare open C with the three-note C voicing.
Inspect F and G note order and excluded strings.
Compare the A-major and A-minor third.
State the rule and its power/seventh-chord exceptions.

criteria: I can name root, third and fifth in C major.
I know repeated strings or octaves do not add distinct chord members.
I can explain why the lowest note of a triad voicing need not name the chord.
I can identify the C#/C difference between A major and A minor.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Name the three chord members and demonstrate one clear three-string voicing, including the major/minor distinction.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Inspect one string at a time and name its note before comparing a larger shape.
selfAssessment.proves: Self-checked triad vocabulary, voicing and listening distinctions.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: A claim that all chords have only three notes, automatic harmonic recognition or three-key recall.

lessons.title: One, Four, Five, Six
lessons.objective: Derive and play I, IV, V and vi in C, G and D major, preserving the minor quality of vi.

steps.title: Derive the first key
steps.action: Read the C-major scale and select roots 1,4,5,6: C,F,G,A. Apply the major-key qualities: C major, F major, G major, A minor. Say C, F, G, A-minor before forming shapes.
steps.lookCheck: Uppercase I,IV,V are major; lowercase vi is minor. The title’s six means a scale degree, not a major VI chord.
steps.listenCheck: Play each chord’s three notes separately so the third is audible.

steps.title: Play a four-chord cycle
steps.action: Use the top-three-string diagrams for C, F, G and Am. Play each once and allow an unhurried pause for the next shape; a metronome is optional here.
steps.lookCheck: Exclude strings 6–4, including open basses that belong to larger shapes. Release between attempts if the mini barre tightens.
steps.listenCheck: Hear three clear notes for every chord; a memorized root name alone is not a played triad.

steps.title: Transfer the numbers to G
steps.action: Use G,A,B,C,D,E,F#. The required chords are G,C,D,Em. Find each root in the scale, say its quality, then use the matching diagram.
steps.lookCheck: The V chord D contains F#, not F. Em may use the three open top strings G,B,E.
steps.listenCheck: Compare D major with an accidental D-minor sound; check string 1 fret 2 if its third is wrong.

steps.title: Transfer to D
steps.action: Use D,E,F#,G,A,B,C#. The required chords are D,G,A,Bm. Name the four first, then play their three-string voicings.
steps.lookCheck: A contains C#; Bm contains D and F#. Keep Bm minor rather than guessing a major shape from its letter name.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for clear thirds in A and Bm, without an extra open string changing the voicing.

steps.title: Retrieve instead of copying
steps.action: Choose one key, cover the key map and named diagrams, say the four chord names, then play them. Uncover afterward to check names, quality and notes. Repeat with another key.
steps.lookCheck: You may study the maps between rounds. A looked-up answer is review, not chart-free recall.
steps.listenCheck: Keep naming accuracy separate from buzzing or muted strings; fix the dimension that actually failed.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I name a major sixth chord.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Write lowercase vi beside scale degree 6, and say the minor suffix aloud: Am, Em or Bm in these keys.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I carry the C-key chord names into G.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Restart from the G-major scale and select roots 1,4,5,6 before choosing shapes.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I know the names but cannot form Bm.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Practise strings 3–1 at 4,3,2 slowly, pick each note, then place it back into the D-key cycle.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I play quickly enough to hide a dead third.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Remove the pulse temporarily and inspect the three notes. This exercise prioritizes correct construction and recall.

practiceSegments.instruction: Derive and play C,F,G,Am.
Derive and play G,C,D,Em.
Derive and play D,G,A,Bm.
Cover the answers for short naming-then-playing retrieval rounds.
Repair one naming error and one physical voicing issue separately.

criteria: I derive the correct four chords in C, G and D major.
I say the minor suffix for vi in every key.
I can play the intended three-string voicings and inspect their thirds.
I know which answers were retrieved and which required the chart.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Name and play each four-chord set with study support as needed, then prepare for a fresh chart-free check.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Rebuild the scale-degree roots and quality pattern before repeating the matching voicing.
selfAssessment.proves: Self-reported chord derivation, triad practice and retrieval preparation in three named keys.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Universal any-key fluency, automated chord recognition or completed chart-free recall when answers were visible.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: Three Keys, Named and Played
lessons.sourceTitle: Checkpoint: Three Keys, Named and Played
lessons.objective: Name I, IV, V and vi first, then play the four chords from memory in each of C, G and D major.

steps.title: Prepare a chart-free round
steps.action: Review the three keys once, then cover the key map and every named chord diagram, or turn the screen away. Use C, G and D in that order for the first check; a later practice round can change the order.
steps.lookCheck: The target is three keys and twelve chord responses. There is no required speed, timed-answer percentage or automatic random key caller.
steps.listenCheck: Confirm tuning before hiding the references so pitch preparation does not interrupt the recall round.

steps.title: Name the four before playing
steps.action: For C major, say the names of I, IV, V and vi aloud before touching the first shape. Do the same when moving to G and D. Keep the minor suffix explicit.
steps.lookCheck: Do not use the shape you happen to form as a cue for guessing its name afterward. No written answers or partner chord prompts during the round.
steps.listenCheck: Say each name distinctly enough to remember whether you said major or minor.

steps.title: Play and inspect each response
steps.action: After naming a key’s four chords, form each taught three-string voicing in that order. Pick strings 3,2,1 separately, then strum them together. Take a reasonable untimed pause to place the fingers.
steps.lookCheck: Keep strings 6–4 excluded. Each response requires a recalled chord identity and a played voicing, not only the root note.
steps.listenCheck: Hear all three intended notes, including the quality-defining third. A buzz or wrong note means that played response needs repair.

steps.title: Complete all three keys before looking
steps.action: Continue through C, G and D without consulting the charts. After stopping, uncover the table and verify all twelve names and played voicings; state any prompt, correction or uncertain response.
steps.lookCheck: Correcting a name after looking is learning, but does not rewrite that recall attempt. Do not combine the best key from three different rounds.
steps.listenCheck: Recall success and clean playing must both be supported by your own review; neither is inferred from elapsed time.

steps.title: Report the actual scope
steps.action: Claim the three-key target only when all twelve chord identities and voicings were recalled in one chart-free round. Otherwise name the exact key, degree or string to practise before a new round.
steps.lookCheck: These are the three taught keys. Passing them does not establish every major key or all triad inversions.
steps.listenCheck: Revisit the weakest quality contrast, such as A versus Am or the F# inside D, before repeating.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I forget the minor suffix but play a minor shape.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Treat the naming response as needing review. Practise naming and playing as two explicit steps.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I need one quick diagram glance for Bm.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Keep the round as supported practice, repair Bm, then start a fresh full round without charts.

mistakeRecovery.observation: Every chord name is correct but one string is consistently dead.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Repair that voicing string by string. Names alone do not meet the named-and-played target.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I pass a different key in each separate attempt.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Keep those as progress, then make one new round containing all three keys; do not splice results.

practiceSegments.instruction: Check tuning, review the rules and cover the key map and diagrams.
Name then play the four responses in C major.
Name then play the four responses in G major.
Name then play the four responses in D major.
Uncover references and review all twelve responses honestly.
State the achieved scope or the exact repair before the next round.

criteria: I named the four chords before playing each key’s set.
C gave C,F,G,Am; G gave G,C,D,Em; D gave D,G,A,Bm.
I played all twelve taught three-string voicings and heard their intended notes.
One complete round used no chart, diagram glance or supplied chord-name prompt.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: One chart-free round contains all twelve correctly named and played chord responses across C, G and D major.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Keep the failed naming or voicing response, repair it with the chart, then make a new complete round.
selfAssessment.proves: Self-reported naming and playing recall for the three specifically taught keys.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: An automatic recall score, microphone verification, fluency in every key or mastery of every inversion.

lessons.title: One Shape, Twelve Chords
lessons.objective: Move an E-based major/minor grip with a sixth-string root and understand what the index barre replaces.

steps.title: Find the movable root
steps.action: Recall open E major, then use middle, ring and little fingers so the index is free. The index takes the role of the nut when the shape moves; the lowest note on string 6 names the chord.
steps.lookCheck: Read G major at fret 3 in the diagram. All fret positions move together; no open string remains in this full shape.
steps.listenCheck: Pick the low G first, then the remaining notes one at a time.

steps.title: Build G major briefly
steps.action: Index barres fret 3; ring and little finger use strings 5/4 fret 5; middle uses string 3 fret 4. Check all six strings, strum once, then mute and release.
steps.lookCheck: Keep the guitar supported and make small placement adjustments near the fret wires. Do not clamp continuously for the whole practice block.
steps.listenCheck: Hear every intended note, especially the high strings under the index and the middle-finger third.

steps.title: Change the quality
steps.action: Lift the middle finger so the index sounds string 3 at fret 3. Recheck that string and the rest of the grip: this is G minor.
steps.lookCheck: Only the third changes from B to B-flat; the root and fifth stay in place.
steps.listenCheck: Compare G major and G minor as two qualities, not merely different volumes.

steps.title: Connect shape and names
steps.action: Read the root table at frets 1,3,5,7,8: F,G,A,B,C. A one-fret movement transposes the grip by one semitone; twelve frets repeats the note names an octave higher.
steps.lookCheck: The title refers to transposing this chord family, not to every possible chord type or twelve new fingerings.
steps.listenCheck: Name the root before you sound it, then check quality separately.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The index makes some strings clear and others dead.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Release and move the barre slightly toward the fret wire, then test the failing string alone. Do not solve every buzz with greater force.

mistakeRecovery.observation: My minor grip still sounds major.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Check string 3: it should sound at the barre fret after the middle finger lifts.

mistakeRecovery.observation: Moving up the neck leaves an open string ringing.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Mute before the move, reduce pressure without flicking a string, then settle the new grip before picking.

practiceSegments.instruction: Locate the root and compare the movable grip with open E.
Build and release G major with six-string checks.
Compare G major and minor, inspecting the third.
Name the five selected root positions and recap transposition.

criteria: I know the root is on string 6.
I can describe the index replacing the nut for this closed shape.
I can identify which note changes major to minor.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Explain the grip and make a short, comfortable G-major/G-minor comparison with each string checked.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Repair the weakest barre contact in short attempts and revisit partial-F work if needed.
selfAssessment.proves: Self-checked movable-shape understanding and initial tone comparison.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: All-position fluency, automatic recognition, a timed strength test or mastery of every chord type.

lessons.title: Five Positions, Clean
lessons.objective: Check E-shape major and minor at five named roots without carrying tension from one attempt to the next.

steps.title: Use a manageable order
steps.action: Work frets 5,3,7,8,1 for A,G,B,C,F. Begin where the strings feel manageable and include fret 1 only in short attempts. At each root, inspect major and minor separately.
steps.lookCheck: Use the same six-string voicings throughout; a partial chord is useful preparation but not a full-barre response.
steps.listenCheck: Name the root before strumming so moving the grip does not become blind shape sliding.

steps.title: Check one quality completely
steps.action: From fingers released, form the major grip. Pick strings 6 through 1, identify any buzz or dead note, then strum and mute. Rest briefly before a new entry.
steps.lookCheck: Look for fingertip clearance and index contact at each new fret spacing. Do not hold the shape while repairing several attempts and count them as fresh entries.
steps.listenCheck: A loud low string must not cover an inaudible upper string.

steps.title: Change to minor and compare
steps.action: Rebuild the minor grip at the same root. Listen especially to string 3 under the index; then inspect all six notes and release.
steps.lookCheck: Middle finger stays clear of the minor third; the barre remains at the stated fret.
steps.listenCheck: Compare the two qualities before moving on, checking clarity independently from the name.

steps.title: Record a specific repair
steps.action: For each root, note major/minor and the first problem string. Revisit that grip after resting instead of repeating every comfortable position again.
steps.lookCheck: All ten combinations are practice targets, not a required ten-chord endurance run.
steps.listenCheck: Notice whether a small position change fixes the sound more effectively than extra pressure.

mistakeRecovery.observation: Fret 1 requires an uncomfortable grip.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Stop and reset support. Use shorter partial preparation before returning to full F; do not substitute it in a completed five-position result.

mistakeRecovery.observation: Minor chords lose string 3.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Test the index contact on that string before adding the ring/little fingers.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I slide quickly over difficult positions.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Stop the tempo work and inspect each string; there is no speed target here.

practiceSegments.instruction: Read the five roots and choose the practice order.
Check major grips at all five positions with rests.
Check minor grips and compare the thirds.
Repair the weakest position and string.
State which of the ten combinations still needs work.

criteria: I attempted both qualities at all five roots.
I checked every intended string rather than only the low root.
I can name the weakest quality/position/string combination.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Complete deliberate checks of the ten combinations, keeping any failed grip visible as a repair before the checkpoint.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Isolate the failing string and repeat a fresh short entry after rest.
selfAssessment.proves: Self-reported five-position accuracy practice and repair observations.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: A random-call assessment, verified clean tone or completion when a full grip was replaced by a partial shape.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: Major and Minor at Five Positions
lessons.sourceTitle: Checkpoint: Major and Minor at Five Positions
lessons.objective: Recall and check all ten E-shape major/minor combinations at the five selected frets in mixed order.

steps.title: Prepare the ten prompts
steps.action: Write each fret 1,3,5,7,8 paired with major and minor on separate slips, then shuffle them, or ask a partner to mix them. No automatic random caller is provided.
steps.lookCheck: Every pair appears once; avoid selecting only the easy roots. Cover the diagrams after preparation.
steps.listenCheck: You may hear a partner’s fret and quality prompt, but they should not tell you the fingering.

steps.title: Respond from a released hand
steps.action: For each prompt, name the chord, form it, and pick all six strings individually before a short strum. Mute and release before drawing the next prompt.
steps.lookCheck: The stated fret belongs to the index and root on string 6. Middle finger decides the major/minor third.
steps.listenCheck: Every intended string must ring without an obvious dead note or buzz.

steps.title: Keep failures in the round
steps.action: If you repair the held shape, note the failed response. Use the repair to learn, then begin a later fresh round rather than replacing only its misses with successes.
steps.lookCheck: Ten fresh responses make one round. A partial voicing or changed fret is not an equivalent response.
steps.listenCheck: Keep the chord-name/quality check separate from the tone check.

steps.title: Apply the complete target
steps.action: Review all ten responses. Claim the five-position major-and-minor target only when the complete mixed round met the naming and six-string criteria comfortably.
steps.lookCheck: No timing deadline or endurance requirement; rests between responses are allowed.
steps.listenCheck: If a string’s clarity was uncertain, keep that response for review rather than assuming it was clean.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The correct root has the wrong quality.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Review the third on string 3, then start a fresh full round after practising that distinction.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I passed only four positions.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Keep the result as partial practice. The stated target includes all five positions in both qualities.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I used diagrams during the response.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Call it supported practice and repeat without fingering references when ready.

practiceSegments.instruction: Prepare and mix the ten fret/quality prompts.
Name, form, inspect and release all ten responses with rests.
Review failures by position, quality and string.
Repair one grip and state whether the complete target was met.

criteria: The round included both qualities at frets 1,3,5,7,8.
I named each prompted chord and recalled its grip without a diagram.
All six intended strings were clear in each fresh response.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: One complete mixed round contains ten correctly named, clearly sounded major/minor responses.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Keep the failed combination, repair it, then make a new full round without replacing misses inside the old one.
selfAssessment.proves: Learner-reported recall and six-string clarity across the ten specified grips.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: App-generated random calls, measured recall percentage, microphone-certified chord quality or all-neck mastery.

lessons.title: The Second Movable Shape
lessons.objective: Build a five-string A-shape major barre and use its fifth-string root alongside the E-shape family.

steps.title: Move the root to string 5
steps.action: Read C major as an A-shape barre at fret 3. Index spans strings 5–1; middle, ring and little fingers use strings 4,3,2 at fret 5. Exclude string 6.
steps.lookCheck: The root is now C on string 5, not G on string 6 at the same fret.
steps.listenCheck: Pick from string 5 and hear the intended C-major notes without a low G beneath them.

steps.title: Keep the top string clear
steps.action: Use three separate fingertips for the fret-5 cluster. Let the index sound string 1 at fret 3. Check each of the five intended strings before strumming.
steps.lookCheck: Do not force a ring-finger joint backward to make a second barre. If the top string is omitted during preparation, label that a four-string version.
steps.listenCheck: A full response here includes the clear high G on string 1.

steps.title: Compare two root locations
steps.action: Play G with an E-shape root at fret 3, then C with an A-shape root at fret 3. Release pressure during the change and move the picking start to string 5.
steps.lookCheck: Both index positions use fret 3, but the finger cluster and allowed string group change.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for the root change rather than judging only whether the hand moved a long distance.

steps.title: Define the useful scope
steps.action: Transpose the A-shape root to D at 5 and E at 7. Together with E-shape roots, these major-chord families offer nearby choices; additional qualities and extensions still need their own fingerings.
steps.lookCheck: Two families do not literally cover every possible chord. Name the quality and root explicitly.
steps.listenCheck: Compare one clean voicing at a time, with a released hand between checks.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The index root stays on string 6.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Say fifth-string root and start the pick on string 5; mute the low string before the next attempt.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The cluster mutes the high string.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Curve the three separate fingertips and inspect string 1 alone. Do not count a four-string version as the taught full five-string shape.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I squeeze the whole hand to make the cluster fit.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Release and place one finger at a time near the fret wire, with short attempts and comfortable support.

practiceSegments.instruction: Locate the C root and read the five-string grip.
Inspect C major’s five strings and release between entries.
Alternate E-shape G with A-shape C.
Move the A-shape root to D and E and state its scope.

criteria: I identify the fifth-string root of the A shape.
I can explain the excluded low string and the intended high string.
I can distinguish the two major-grip families at the same fret.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Build and inspect a brief five-string C-major A-shape grip, then explain its difference from E-shape G.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Repair one cluster or barre contact, keeping reduced voicings labelled as preparation.
selfAssessment.proves: Self-checked A-shape placement and root-location understanding.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Every chord quality, automatic voicing recognition or a full progression performance.

lessons.title: Barre-Chord Song, Both Shapes
lessons.objective: Play Crossings, a complete original sixteen-bar piece that switches between E-shape G and A-shape C/D.

steps.title: Read the complete map
steps.action: Use the Crossings panels and three diagrams. Each bar has downstrokes on 1 and 3, with notes sustained for two beats. Begin with a separate quarter-note metronome around 60 BPM.
steps.lookCheck: Keep the map visible, or copy it before opening a separate native metronome sheet. No synchronized backing is provided.
steps.listenCheck: Sound G,C,D separately and inspect their intended string groups.

steps.title: Isolate the family change
steps.action: Loop one G bar into one C bar, then G into D. Lighten pressure just before the next downbeat, move the cluster, and start the pick on the correct root string.
steps.lookCheck: G sounds all six strings; C/D begin on string 5. Do not drag fully pressed fingers across the neck.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for a clean next downbeat without an open-string sweep.

steps.title: Join the four-bar sections
steps.action: Play bars 1–4, 5–8, 9–12 and 13–16 as separate rehearsal sections, retaining four beats per bar. Repair the C-to-D change without shortening a bar.
steps.lookCheck: The ending is C,D,G,G, not another copy of the opening.
steps.listenCheck: Keep the same half-note spacing through repeated chords and movement.

steps.title: Play the full piece
steps.action: After four count-in beats, play all sixteen bars and 32 attacks in order. Mute after the final bar’s fourth beat. Record actual tempo, continuity and any problem change separately.
steps.lookCheck: A restart or omitted bar makes the take interrupted; finishing the panels is not a performed take.
steps.listenCheck: The last G should have the same pulse and clarity as the first.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The pick catches string 6 on C or D.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Practise the new picking start with muted strings, then restore the chord.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The C-to-D slide delays the attack.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Move with released pressure at a slower click, then reconnect the preceding bar.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I lose the final section.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Read C,D,G,G aloud and practise bars 11–16 before the next full take.

practiceSegments.instruction: Read all sixteen bars and inspect the three shapes.
Loop the two grip-family changes slowly.
Practise the four-bar sections.
Play the complete map with a count-in and review continuity.
State actual tempo and one precise repair.

criteria: I played the complete sixteen-bar order.
I switched picking roots and finger clusters correctly.
I kept two attacks and four beats per bar and reported interruptions honestly.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Play the full original piece at a controllable tempo and identify any remaining tone or change repair.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Loop the first failing two-bar change, then return to the complete form.
selfAssessment.proves: Self-reported performance of the original written piece at the stated tempo.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Automatic backing playback, recorded study transport, microphone chord scoring or a commercial-song performance.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: One-Four-Five, Both Shapes
lessons.objective: Play I–IV–V–I in G, A and C using the specified nearby E- and A-shape roots.

steps.title: Read the three routes
steps.action: Use the nearby-key guide. In each key, I uses an E-shape root; IV and V use A-shape roots. The index roots stay within a two-fret span.
steps.lookCheck: G uses roots 3,3,5; A uses 5,5,7; C uses 8,8,10. The root string is part of the address.
steps.listenCheck: Name all three major chords in a key before playing.

steps.title: Play a four-bar cycle
steps.action: For each key, use one four-beat bar each of I,IV,V,I and one downstroke on every beat 1. Choose a comfortable unchanged tempo, leaving each chord ringing for its bar.
steps.lookCheck: Inspect the intended six or five strings before the check. The high A-shape string is part of this version.
steps.listenCheck: The quality remains major for all three chords; a missed third is not hidden by the root.

steps.title: Connect both families
steps.action: On each change, release excess pressure, place the next root and cluster, then pick from the right starting string. Complete all three key cycles with short rests between them.
steps.lookCheck: No need to optimize every possible fingering; this check uses the explicitly taught nearby route.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for a steady bar length and a clean return from V to I.

steps.title: Review the full scope
steps.action: State whether G, A and C all met the shape, chord-name and timing rules. Keep any reduced voicing, wrong root or stopped cycle as practice to repair.
steps.lookCheck: One complete check includes all three keys; do not combine the best key from unrelated incomplete rounds.
steps.listenCheck: Separate a correct name from a clearly sounded chord.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I play IV with the old sixth-string root.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Locate the same fret on string 5, then rebuild the A-shape cluster.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The root span is small but the grip is tense.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Use lighter pressure during movement and allow rests between key cycles; small travel does not require a rigid hand.

mistakeRecovery.observation: One key is missing from my result.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Keep it partial and practise that key before a new complete check.

practiceSegments.instruction: Name and inspect the three nearby key routes.
Play the G-major four-bar cycle.
Play the A-major cycle.
Play the C-major cycle.
Review all three and repair the weakest change.
State the completed scope or remaining key.

criteria: I used I,IV,V,I correctly in G,A,C.
Each cycle used the specified E/A families and root strings.
I kept four beats per bar with clear intended strings.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: All three four-bar key cycles meet the named-chord, full-voicing and steady-bar conditions in one reviewed check.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Repair the failed root-string/cluster change slowly and repeat the complete three-key check.
selfAssessment.proves: Self-reported I–IV–V application using a defined nearby route in three keys.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Automatic recall scoring, a globally minimal-motion proof, all-key fluency or microphone-certified tone.

lessons.title: The Neck Is One Scale
lessons.objective: See five overlapping CAGED regions as the same G-major notes and locate roots and shared positions.

steps.title: Name one collection
steps.action: Read G,A,B,C,D,E,F#. The five map panels show this same collection through E,D,C,A,G chord-form regions; they do not change the key.
steps.lookCheck: F# is the only sharp in this key. Every listed fret has its note name beside it.
steps.listenCheck: Play G on string 1 fret 3, then A on 5, and hear the beginning of the collection.

steps.title: Read one string at a time
steps.action: Start with the E view, frets 2–5. Pick one listed note at a time on one string, then move to the next string. Do not strum the list as a chord.
steps.lookCheck: A panel is a fret map, not a command to stretch across the entire window at once.
steps.listenCheck: Check that the notes match the named scale, especially F# rather than F.

steps.title: Find roots and overlaps
steps.action: Find G at the listed root addresses. Compare two adjacent views and point to a fret present in both. That shared address is literally the same note, not a new scale degree.
steps.lookCheck: The views overlap; using a shared note helps you move between them.
steps.listenCheck: Sound the same shared fret twice before moving to a neighbouring note.

steps.title: Preview all five views
steps.action: Read each panel and locate a G within it. Explore only a few notes in unfamiliar higher regions today, moving the hand instead of forcing a span. The next lesson connects the first three.
steps.lookCheck: The CAGED labels describe familiar chord-form landmarks; do not infer a different mode from which note you start.
steps.listenCheck: Hear the common G home pitch across octaves and registers.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I treat each panel as a different key.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Recite G,A,B,C,D,E,F# again and compare the same note in two panels.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The many fret numbers look like a chord.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Choose one string and pick its numbers in order as single notes; never hold the full panel at once.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I confuse fret 4 with scale degree 4.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Read the note name beside the fret. In G major the fourth degree is C, regardless of fret number.

practiceSegments.instruction: Name the seven G-major notes.
Explore the E view string by string.
Find roots and shared notes between adjacent views.
Preview the remaining regions without forced reaches.
Explain why the five views stay in one key.

criteria: I name G-major’s seven notes and its F#.
I can locate a G root and a shared fret in adjacent views.
I know a fret map is single-note material, not a chord grip.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Explain the shared collection and demonstrate one overlap plus a root in each inspected region.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Return to one string, name its notes, and connect only two overlapping maps first.
selfAssessment.proves: Self-checked fretboard-map understanding and pitch-location exploration.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Five memorized full patterns, measured scale fluency, automatic position recognition or a tempo result.

lessons.title: Connect Three Positions
lessons.objective: Connect E-, D- and C-region hand positions using the written four-bar G-major route without adding time for a shift.

steps.title: Read the route and fingers
steps.action: Use the sixteen-note route and hand-position panels. One note occupies each quarter beat. The route deliberately crosses the first three regions and returns.
steps.lookCheck: Follow the stated finger changes: E view on 3/5, D view on 7/8, C view on 10/8/7. Shared frets can use different fingers after a shift.
steps.listenCheck: Tap individual note references if useful, then let them stop before you play.

steps.title: Isolate the first connection
steps.action: Play frets 3,5,7,8 slowly. Release pressure after fret 5 and move the hand so ring reaches 7 and little reaches 8. Keep the intended note order.
steps.lookCheck: The movement happens between attacks, not by adding an extra beat or stretching the little finger from the old position.
steps.listenCheck: Hear four distinct notes with no accidental open string or dragged extra attack.

steps.title: Connect to the C region and back
steps.action: Practise 8 to 10, then 10,8,7,5 using the written new fingers. Make the final return from 7 to 3 in bar 4 a separate slow fragment.
steps.lookCheck: Each fragment retains its original number of beats once you restore the click. Preparation pauses are allowed only outside a full take.
steps.listenCheck: Listen to the landing pitch as well as the gap before it.

steps.title: Run all four bars
steps.action: With a separate quarter-note metronome around 60 BPM, count four lead-in beats and play all sixteen notes. Lower the tempo for a broken shift; the named target later is 100 BPM.
steps.lookCheck: Do not relabel slower practice as a 100-BPM result. This lesson has no automatic position or timing score.
steps.listenCheck: Keep each shift inside the same pulse as the notes that stay in place.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I wait an extra click before fret 10.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Loop 7,8,10 slowly, moving between attacks and retaining three equal note slots.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The slide itself becomes an extra loud note.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Lighten pressure and keep the picking hand still during movement; re-pick only the written target.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I use one tense stretched grip for all three regions.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Stop and follow the finger/position guide with a relaxed whole-hand move.

practiceSegments.instruction: Read the sixteen-note route and three finger regions.
Loop the E-to-D connection.
Loop the D-to-C and return shifts.
Play full four-bar routes at a controllable tempo.
State actual tempo and the first shift requiring repair.

criteria: I followed the written sixteen notes and hand-position guide.
I can move between regions without extending the bar during a practice take.
I report the actual working tempo and any restart.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Play a complete four-bar route at a controllable tempo with all three planned hand regions; use the checkpoint for 100 BPM.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Slow the exact shift plus its preceding/following note, then reconnect the original rhythm.
selfAssessment.proves: Self-reported position-connection practice on the defined route.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Microphone-scored note/timing accuracy, detected fingering or a 100-BPM result from slower practice.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: Three Positions at One Hundred
lessons.sourceTitle: Checkpoint: Three Positions at One Hundred
lessons.objective: Play the complete sixteen-note connection at 100 BPM using all three taught regions and an unbroken quarter-note pulse.

steps.title: Set the exact target
steps.action: Use the same route and fingers. Set a separate metronome to 100 BPM with one click per quarter note; inspect the starting notes before the take.
steps.lookCheck: The sixteen notes fill four bars. One click is one written note, not two notes or a half-speed interpretation.
steps.listenCheck: Hear four even count-in beats before beginning.

steps.title: Play the four-bar route
steps.action: Play each written fret on its beat, including the shifts into D and C regions and the final return to G at fret 3. Hold the last note for its full beat.
steps.lookCheck: Do not add a preparation beat, omit a target, or play the route entirely in one stretched hand position.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for the landing pitch and attack aligning with the click at each shift.

steps.title: Keep the take intact
steps.action: If a note is late, wrong or lost, retain the attempt as practice and identify its bar/beat. Repair afterward and begin a new count-in for a fresh full take.
steps.lookCheck: Do not stitch accurate fragments into one claimed continuous route.
steps.listenCheck: A correct final G does not erase a wrong or delayed earlier landing.

steps.title: Review sound and movement separately
steps.action: State whether all sixteen notes and their spacing were correct, whether all three intended positions were used, and whether the actual tempo was 100.
steps.lookCheck: These are self-observations. The app does not verify hand position or score this route.
steps.listenCheck: If the click/attack relationship was uncertain, repeat a smaller fragment before another full attempt.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The metronome says 100 but I wait two clicks per note.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Restore one note per quarter-note click; a half-speed interpretation does not meet this route’s target.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The gap occurs only at the final return.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Loop bar 4 slowly with its exact four notes, then restore the full four-bar take.

mistakeRecovery.observation: A pitch reference played during my take.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Stop the reference and restart. Reference sound is not your performance evidence.

practiceSegments.instruction: Set 100 BPM and inspect the route/finger plan.
Warm up the two shifts and final return.
Make fresh full four-bar takes with separate count-ins.
Repair the first failed note or timing gap.
State actual tempo, sound and position observations.

criteria: I used 100 BPM with one note per click.
All sixteen written notes filled four intact bars without a gap or restart.
I used the E,D,C regions and the stated return fingering.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: One complete self-reviewed route meets the note, pulse and position conditions at 100 BPM.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Keep the actual error and working tempo, repair the fragment and retry a fresh full route.
selfAssessment.proves: Learner-reported sixteen-note connection at the stated tempo.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Automated pitch/timing score, position detection, five-pattern mastery or other routes at 100 BPM.

lessons.title: Phrasing Over the Changes
lessons.objective: Plan an eight-bar phrase around changes in G, Em, C and D, hearing each new chord as a destination.

steps.title: Read the harmony before the scale
steps.action: Use G,G,Em,Em,C,C,D,D, one chord per bar. The chord changes at bars 3,5,7 after the initial G at bar 1. Name each chord’s root, third and fifth.
steps.lookCheck: The key is G major; F# belongs to D. This is not the earlier A-blues palette.
steps.listenCheck: Play or hear each chord from the existing diagrams before choosing lead notes.

steps.title: Choose four destinations
steps.action: Pick one chord tone for each arrival, starting with the thirds B,G,E,F#. Find these on string 1 at frets 7,3,0,2.
steps.lookCheck: An arrival is a note at the correct bar and beat, not simply a note that appeared somewhere in the solo.
steps.listenCheck: Hold each destination long enough to hear it with its chord.

steps.title: Make space between arrivals
steps.action: Use short G-major ideas or deliberate rests between destination bars. Keep counting all eight bars while leaving room for the next change.
steps.lookCheck: More notes are not required. Plan the next arrival before filling the remaining beats.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for a phrase that leads toward the next harmony rather than continuing an unrelated scale run.

steps.title: Use an actual harmonic context
steps.action: Play with a partner or your own separate recording of the eight-bar map. Without accompaniment, rehearse the destination schedule with a click and label it preparation.
steps.lookCheck: No supplied backing or automatic chord-tone analysis is implied.
steps.listenCheck: Hear whether each destination belongs to the chord that is actually sounding.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I keep using C natural as if this were A blues.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Return to the G-major chord map; C is available in the key but is not a chord tone of G or D.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I arrive after the change.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Practise only a destination on each arrival bar’s first beat before adding fills.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I lose the form during a rest.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Count the two-bar chord spans aloud and re-enter on the planned next beat.

practiceSegments.instruction: Read and sound the four harmonies.
Find four destination tones.
Create short phrases and counted rests between them.
Place the plan over actual accompaniment if available.
State which arrivals were clear and what support was used.

criteria: I know the eight-bar harmonic order.
I can choose a chord tone for each arrival.
I keep counting through space and distinguish accompaniment from click-only practice.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Explain the four destinations and rehearse an eight-bar plan with clear arrival points.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Remove fills and play only the destinations until the form is secure.
selfAssessment.proves: Self-checked harmonic planning and phrase structure.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Automatic chord-tone detection, measured continuity or over-harmony performance with no accompaniment.

lessons.title: Target the Third
lessons.objective: Land on the third of each chord at bars 1,3,5,7, then connect those targets with short G-major phrases.

steps.title: Name the thirds
steps.action: Say B for G, G for Em, E for C, F# for D. Sound the four reference pitches separately, then stop reference playback before your own practice.
steps.lookCheck: The third is counted from each chord root, not always scale degree 3 of the overall key.
steps.listenCheck: Compare the minor third of Em with the major thirds of the other chords.

steps.title: Play only arrivals first
steps.action: At a comfortable pulse, play string 1 fret 7 at bar 1, 3 at bar 3, open at bar 5 and 2 at bar 7. Hold each for at least the first beat; count the remaining beats and bars.
steps.lookCheck: The target schedule spans eight bars, not four quick quarter notes.
steps.listenCheck: Each arrival should be heard on the first beat of its new chord.

steps.title: Add one small connection
steps.action: Between two arrivals, add two or three G-major notes or a rest, then return to the next scheduled third. Repeat each two-bar span before joining all eight.
steps.lookCheck: Do not let a fill take the space reserved for the next arrival.
steps.listenCheck: Hear how the third identifies the current chord instead of choosing notes only by proximity.

steps.title: Play and review with harmony
steps.action: Use a partner or separate self-made accompaniment of the exact map. After a take, identify each arrival as on time/correct, late, wrong or uncertain.
steps.lookCheck: Without accompaniment this is schedule rehearsal; no automatic arrival score is created.
steps.listenCheck: Keep arrival quality separate from how many notes you played between changes.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I play B over every chord because the key is G.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Recalculate each chord’s own third and rehearse its note by name before adding the click.

mistakeRecovery.observation: A busy fill pushes out the next target.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Shorten the fill and leave a rest before the arrival.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The open E rings into the next F# target.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: End the previous note cleanly and pick the fretted F# on its intended first beat.

practiceSegments.instruction: Name and sound the four thirds.
Rehearse only the eight-bar arrival schedule.
Add short connections and planned rests.
Join all eight bars with known accompaniment when available.
Review the four arrivals separately.

criteria: I identify each chord’s own third.
I land the thirds at bars 1,3,5,7 rather than at arbitrary times.
I leave enough space to preserve the next arrival.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Demonstrate the scheduled thirds and connect them through an eight-bar rehearsal, stating whether harmony was present.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Return to arrival-only playing for the first failed change, then restore a shorter fill.
selfAssessment.proves: Self-reported third-target practice and harmonic listening.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: A measured chord-tone result, automatic backing playback or a guarantee of solo quality.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: Eight Bars, Chord Tones Landed
lessons.sourceTitle: Checkpoint: Eight Bars, Chord Tones Landed
lessons.objective: Improvise through eight complete bars with a correct planned chord-tone arrival at every new harmony.

steps.title: Choose targets and accompaniment
steps.action: Use actual accompaniment for G,G,Em,Em,C,C,D,D. State one root, third or fifth for each of G,Em,C,D before the take. Thirds are useful but not mandatory for this checkpoint.
steps.lookCheck: The four assessed arrivals are bars 1,3,5,7 on beat 1. No backing means click-only preparation, not a complete harmonic check.
steps.listenCheck: Hear the starting G and confirm the exact bar order.

steps.title: Play the full eight bars
steps.action: After the agreed count-in, improvise with the G-major collection and land each stated destination on its arrival beat, holding at least one beat. Count through intentional rests.
steps.lookCheck: Keep all eight bars; do not pause the accompaniment or restart after a missed note.
steps.listenCheck: The destination must belong to the sounding chord, not merely to the overall scale.

steps.title: Finish within the form
steps.action: Complete the phrase by the end of bar 8. Keep the take intact and remember any late, wrong or uncertain arrival.
steps.lookCheck: A recovered later phrase does not erase a missed arrival. Extra note count earns no credit.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for all four clear harmonic landings and a deliberate ending.

steps.title: Review every requirement
steps.action: State continuity, the four arrival results and actual accompaniment use. Claim the target only when the complete take met them all.
steps.lookCheck: This is a self-review, not an app-measured chord-tone arrival score.
steps.listenCheck: If a landing was hard to hear, repeat that two-bar transition before the next full attempt.

mistakeRecovery.observation: All the notes are in G major but one landing clashes.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Check that landing against the current chord’s root/third/fifth, then practise it with that chord alone.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I miss the first beat but reach the right note later.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Keep that arrival late. Rehearse an earlier preparation rest and retry the full form.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I play four good bars twice.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Keep the fragments as practice; the checkpoint needs one continuous eight-bar take.

practiceSegments.instruction: Confirm accompaniment and choose four target tones.
Warm up the arrival schedule without fills.
Make full eight-bar attempts with fresh count-ins.
Review and repair the first missed arrival.
State complete, partial or unverified conditions.

criteria: The exact accompaniment continued for all eight bars.
I landed the four declared chord tones on beat 1 of bars 1,3,5,7.
I kept the form through rests without a restart or skipped bar.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: One self-reviewed eight-bar improvisation contains all four correct on-time arrivals and uninterrupted form awareness.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Practise the first failed arrival with fewer fill notes, then make a new full take.
selfAssessment.proves: Learner-reported eight-bar continuity and four harmonic arrivals.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Automated chord-tone analysis, microphone timing certification, artistic evaluation or a full result without accompaniment.

lessons.title: Hear It, Hum It, Find It
lessons.sourceTitle: Hear It, Hum It, Find It
lessons.objective: Hear a short phrase, keep its contour by humming, then find and write its notes without looking at an answer first.

steps.title: Separate listening from reading
steps.action: Use a helper for the original four-note prompt below while you look away from its answer panel and the helper’s fretting hand. If you already read the key, call this familiar-phrase practice.
steps.lookCheck: No hidden-answer audio player is supplied. The helper performs the written prompt accurately.
steps.listenCheck: Listen once without touching the guitar; notice whether the phrase rises, falls or returns.

steps.title: Keep the sound in memory
steps.action: Hum or sing the shape softly in a comfortable range, using an octave shift if needed. Tap the four even beats without trying to name notes yet.
steps.lookCheck: This is an ear-memory aid, not a vocal-range test or a requirement to imitate guitar register.
steps.listenCheck: Hear the final return and compare it with the starting pitch.

steps.title: Find the first note, then intervals
steps.action: Find a matching guitar pitch, then locate the remaining notes by comparing their direction and distance. Request another identical hearing if the memory fades.
steps.lookCheck: Do not look at the helper key while searching. Guessing many frets at once can replace listening with trial and error.
steps.listenCheck: Compare one found note with the sound you remembered before moving on.

steps.title: Write before revealing
steps.action: Write the four note names/octaves or string/fret addresses and their beats. Keep that first answer, then compare with the helper key and replay the correction.
steps.lookCheck: A corrected answer is review, not the original unseen response.
steps.listenCheck: Identify one missed interval or rhythm rather than simply repeating the entire phrase faster.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I search the fretboard before remembering the phrase.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Put the guitar down and hum the short phrase again first.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The register is uncomfortable to hum.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Use a comfortable octave, then match the correct guitar octave separately.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I saw the answer key first.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Use the known phrase for practice and arrange a different unseen prompt for a fresh ear check.

practiceSegments.instruction: Arrange the helper prompt and avoid its visible answer.
Listen, hum and tap the phrase.
Find the notes by ear on the guitar.
Write and preserve the first response before comparison.
Name the specific ear or rhythm repair.

criteria: I listened without seeing the answer first, or labelled prior familiarity.
I used humming/tapping to retain the phrase before searching.
I preserved a first written response before correction.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Demonstrate the hear–hum–find–write process and explain the difference between first response and review.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Shorten the sound to two notes and reconnect it after retaining the contour.
selfAssessment.proves: Self-reported ear-memory and transcription process practice.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Blind in-app playback, a numeric accuracy score or unseen transcription when the key was already read.

lessons.title: Four Notes From Audio
lessons.objective: Transcribe the original four-note prompt by listening to accurate repeats while its notation stays out of view.

steps.title: Keep the source unseen
steps.action: Ask a helper to use the four-note answer card while you turn away. Do not watch the fretting hand. The helper may repeat the exact phrase; the app has no automatic loop or hidden-notation mode for it.
steps.lookCheck: If the phrase is already known from the concept lesson, label this consolidation practice rather than a fresh test.
steps.listenCheck: Confirm four clear notes at an unchanged quarter-note pulse.

steps.title: Capture rhythm separately
steps.action: Tap four even note lengths and mark their beat positions on paper before choosing pitches. Ask for a repeat only when needed.
steps.lookCheck: Do not confuse the count-in with the four-note phrase.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for where the sound begins and how long each note lasts.

steps.title: Find and order the pitches
steps.action: Hum the phrase, find the first note, then compare each following movement. Write all four notes before the helper reveals the key.
steps.lookCheck: Use exact sounding pitch/octave or string/fret notation; a chord name alone is not a melody transcript.
steps.listenCheck: Check the final note against the first to hear whether the phrase returns.

steps.title: Compare and repair
steps.action: Keep the first response, reveal the answer and compare all four pitches and durations. Re-listen to one missed pair and play it accurately after review.
steps.lookCheck: Do not overwrite the first answer and call the corrected copy a perfect transcription.
steps.listenCheck: A correctly found pitch with the wrong duration still needs a rhythm repair.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I count a lead-in click as the first note.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Have the helper give the same four-count lead-in and mark the phrase start before repeating.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I find the notes but write them in the wrong order.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Hum the complete contour again, then verify each adjacent pair.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I need a fresh accuracy challenge after memorizing the key.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Use the separate four-bar checkpoint prompt without reading its answer, or ask a helper for a different documented unseen phrase outside this fixed exercise.

practiceSegments.instruction: Agree the prompt and whether it is unfamiliar.
Listen and write the four rhythm positions.
Hum, locate and write the ordered pitches.
Compare the preserved first response and repair one interval.
State pitch/rhythm errors and prior familiarity honestly.

criteria: I used repeated actual sound while the answer was out of view.
I wrote four ordered pitches and durations before comparing.
I preserved and reviewed the first response.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Complete a documented four-note transcription practice cycle, with familiarity and mistakes clearly stated.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Re-listen to a shorter pair, retain its contour and then reconnect all four notes.
selfAssessment.proves: Self-reported listening, written response and review of the fixed prompt.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Automatic loops, hidden-notation UI, software-scored transcription or a new unseen result for a memorized phrase.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: Four Bars Transcribed
lessons.objective: Write a first complete four-bar transcription from an accurately performed unseen original phrase, then check pitch and rhythm independently against the 90% target.

steps.title: Protect an unseen source
steps.action: Before reading the helper key below, turn away and have a helper prepare its exact four-bar phrase. If you have already seen it, treat this as familiar-phrase practice; do not claim an unseen score. No blind phrase audio is supplied in the app.
steps.lookCheck: The helper must be able to perform the written notes and rhythm accurately. An uncertain source cannot support a percentage.
steps.listenCheck: Listen to all four bars at a comfortable unchanged tempo after four count-in beats.

steps.title: Transcribe the whole phrase
steps.action: Request accurate repeats of a bar or the full phrase. Hum the contour, tap its quarter/eighth rhythm, and write each note’s pitch/octave or string/fret, onset and duration. Keep four bar lines.
steps.lookCheck: Do not inspect the helper key until the complete first answer is preserved. Twenty note events occupy sixteen beats.
steps.listenCheck: Listen to both the two-eighth-note groups and the longer quarter notes.

steps.title: Score two dimensions after reveal
steps.action: Compare the first answer with the twenty numbered reference events. Count correct pitch+octave out of 20 and correct onset+duration out of 20 separately. At least 18/20 is required in each dimension.
steps.lookCheck: Do not average the two scores to hide a weak dimension. Extra/missing events require form review rather than silent realignment.
steps.listenCheck: A right pitch with a wrong rhythm gets only the pitch point.

steps.title: Apply the validity conditions
steps.action: Keep the score unverified if the source performance was uncertain, the key was seen early, or the first answer was replaced by corrections. Otherwise report both first-answer totals.
steps.lookCheck: This is a helper-reviewed manual rubric; GuitarHub neither captures the transcription nor computes a score.
steps.listenCheck: Compare missed cells against the actual performed source and key, not only what you now expect to hear.

steps.title: Review without rewriting history
steps.action: Correct a second copy and replay the difficult interval or rhythm. Retrying this now-known phrase is review; a future unseen assessment needs a new documented prompt.
steps.lookCheck: The fixed reference remains unchanged across source repeats.
steps.listenCheck: Hear and name the correction you learned, even if the numeric target was not reached.

mistakeRecovery.observation: My pitch total is high but rhythm is below 18.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Keep the target unmet and practise the missed eighth/quarter cells; do not average the totals.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I saw the answer accidentally.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I inserted or omitted notes.

Listen and map four bars of rhythm.
Find the pitches and preserve the complete first transcription.
Reveal and compare pitch and rhythm totals separately.
Report valid/unverified status and review one missed cell.

I preserved all four bars with pitches, onsets and durations.
The first answer earned at least 18/20 pitch and 18/20 rhythm points separately.
