lessons.title: Sixteenths and the Space Between
lessons.objective: Count steady sixteenth subdivisions and create syncopation by sustaining selected off-beat attacks across unplayed downbeats.

steps.title: Separate pulse and subdivision
steps.action: Use a quarter-note click and say 1 e & a through 4 e & a. Four sixteenths fit each beat; keep down-up-down-up movement through the four syllables.
steps.lookCheck: The number and & motions are down; e and a are up. The click marks quarters, not each hand motion.
steps.listenCheck: Hear evenly spaced subdivisions rather than a swung long-short pair.

steps.title: Choose the six contacts
steps.action: Read the cell: play on 1,1a,2&,3,3a,4& only. Start with muted-string hand practice, then use Em. Every other motion passes above the strings.
steps.lookCheck: The physical motion continues even when it makes no new attack.
steps.listenCheck: Hear six actual contacts, not sixteen strums with the extra ten hidden quietly.

steps.title: Keep the written sustains
steps.action: Let the 1a and 3a attacks ring across beats 2 and 4. Those downbeats have no fresh attack, but the chord sound continues.
steps.lookCheck: This differs from the full silent rests of the earlier power-chord piece. Do not mute automatically on 2 and 4.
steps.listenCheck: Hear the off-beat sound carrying through the next strong pulse.

steps.title: Build the cell slowly
steps.action: Loop one bar below 100 BPM, beginning near 50–60 or slower. Add one contact at a time while keeping motion relaxed, then play the complete cell.
steps.lookCheck: Use a separate metronome and keep the pattern visible. No sixteenth scoring or performed demo is supplied.
steps.listenCheck: The skipped attacks and held sounds should be as deliberate as the played strokes.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I swing the e and a subdivisions.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Return to evenly spoken four-part beats at a slower click.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I strike beat 2 after the 1a upstroke.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Keep the next down motion in the air while letting the preceding chord ring.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I mute every missing attack.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Read the sustain rule: this cell omits new contacts while the sound continues.

practiceSegments.instruction: Count and move through even sixteenth subdivisions.
Add the six chosen contacts on muted strings.
Use Em and preserve the written sustains.
Loop the complete one-bar cell slowly.
Explain skipped attack versus full rest.

criteria: I keep sixteen evenly spaced motions per bar.
Only the six written positions contact the strings.
I sustain the off-beat attacks across beats 2 and 4 without new strokes.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Demonstrate the slow complete cell and explain how its off-beat sustains create the syncopated feel.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Remove chord changes and rebuild one beat at a time while maintaining the hand motion.
selfAssessment.proves: Self-checked subdivision and syncopation understanding.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Automatic stroke-direction detection, 100-BPM performance or proof that syncopation is merely silence.

lessons.title: Syncopated Groove Song
lessons.objective: Play After the Line, a complete original twenty-four-bar Em–C–G–D piece using the same syncopated sixteenth cell throughout.

steps.title: Read the full form
steps.action: Use the piece map: two bars each of Em,C,G,D, repeated for three eight-bar sections. Every bar uses the same six-contact cell. Begin at a controllable tempo.
steps.lookCheck: The complete piece is 24 bars, not one eight-bar loop counted three separate times after restarts.
steps.listenCheck: Check the four open chords and keep the intended string groups clear.

steps.title: Maintain the cell through a change
steps.action: Loop the second Em bar into the first C bar. Keep the down/up motion and change chord for the next bar’s first attack without adding a strum. Repeat C-to-G, G-to-D and D-to-Em.
steps.lookCheck: Prepare the fretting move without turning the skipped attacks into extra contact.
steps.listenCheck: The 1a and 3a sustains remain intact before and after the change.

steps.title: Connect sections
steps.action: Play one complete eight-bar section, then connect its final D to the next Em without a pause. Use a separate click and count the section number.
steps.lookCheck: The repeated form does not excuse speeding up. A stopped section remains a rehearsal fragment.
steps.listenCheck: Hear the same quarter pulse across the section boundary.

steps.title: Play and finish the full piece
steps.action: Take four count-in beats and play all 24 bars. In the last bar, make the written 4& attack, hold its remaining half beat, then mute at the next boundary. Record tempo, continuity and the first failed cell.
steps.lookCheck: There are 144 written attacks in the complete piece; the app does not count them for you.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for the final held half beat instead of adding a large extra ending strum.

mistakeRecovery.observation: A chord change inserts a seventh attack.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Loop the boundary slowly with the exact six-contact grid and keep the spare motion in the air.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I restart after each eight bars.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Keep those as section practice, then join two boundaries for a single full form.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The ending arrives early.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Count all of bar 24, including the 4& contact and its final half beat.

practiceSegments.instruction: Read the 24-bar map and check Em,C,G,D.
Loop each two-chord boundary with the full cell.
Join eight-bar sections without a gap.
Play the complete original piece with a fresh count-in.
State tempo, continuity and the exact repair cell.

criteria: I followed all 24 bars and their chord order.
I retained six contacts per bar and the held off-beat notes.
I reported actual tempo and any restart or added attack.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Play the complete written piece at a controllable tempo with a clear account of any remaining rhythmic repair.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Repair the first failed boundary at a slower pulse, then reconnect the full form.
selfAssessment.proves: Self-reported practice of the original 24-bar composition.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Automatic backing playback, measured rhythm accuracy, a 100-BPM checkpoint or a commercial-song arrangement.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: Twenty-Four Bars at One Hundred
lessons.sourceTitle: Checkpoint: Twenty-Four Bars at One Hundred
lessons.objective: Play the complete twenty-four-bar syncopated piece at 100 BPM with its exact attacks, sustains and bar order intact.

steps.title: Set the target exactly
steps.action: Use After the Line and its unchanged one-bar cell. Set a separate metronome to 100 BPM with quarter-note clicks in 4/4, then check the cell on Em before the take.
steps.lookCheck: Sixteenth hand motions subdivide each click into four; do not treat the click as eighths to halve the actual tempo.
steps.listenCheck: Hear the 1a and 3a attacks held across 2 and 4 at the target pulse.

steps.title: Count in and preserve the form
steps.action: After four lead-in beats, play the three eight-bar sections continuously: Em,Em,C,C,G,G,D,D each time. Keep the exact six contacts in every bar.
steps.lookCheck: Twenty-four bars contain 96 quarter-note beats and 144 written attacks; the lead-in is separate.
steps.listenCheck: No extra beat-2 or beat-4 attack should enter as the chord changes.

steps.title: Finish the last full bar
steps.action: Make the final 4& contact in bar 24, sustain its half beat and mute at the next bar line. Keep the take intact when reviewing any drift, wrong contact or skipped bar.
steps.lookCheck: A restart, short bar or omitted attack cannot be repaired invisibly inside a complete result.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for consistent subdivision spacing as well as the overall click alignment.

steps.title: Apply the whole target
steps.action: State the actual tempo and whether every bar retained its contact/sustain pattern with no drift or restart. If any part is uncertain, mark that bar for review and make a fresh attempt later.
steps.lookCheck: This is self-reviewed continuity and rhythm; no automatic sixteenth-pattern score is present.
steps.listenCheck: A loud steady downbeat does not establish that the off-beat placements stayed correct.

mistakeRecovery.observation: 100 is selected but I feel the click twice as fast as my quarter pulse.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Reset the quarter-note interpretation and rehearse one exact bar before another full take.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The final section speeds up.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Practise the bar-16-to-17 boundary with the click and no extra accents, then restart the full form.

mistakeRecovery.observation: I count the right number of strums but their positions are wrong.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Return to the sixteenth grid. Contact timing and sustains matter; a total count alone is insufficient.

practiceSegments.instruction: Set 100 BPM and review the exact grid and full form.
Warm up the hardest chord boundary without changing the cell.
Play a full 24-bar attempt with four count-in beats.
Review the first drift, extra contact or shortened sustain.
Repair that bar and report the actual complete or partial result.

criteria: I used actual 100-BPM quarter-note clicks.
All 24 bars and 144 written contact positions remained intact without a restart.
The off-beat sustains crossed beats 2 and 4 without extra attacks.
I ended after the full final half beat and reported any uncertainty.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: One complete self-reviewed take meets the 100-BPM, 24-bar, exact-pattern and continuity conditions.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Keep the specific failed bar, practise it slower and begin a new complete take when ready.
selfAssessment.proves: Learner-reported performance of the specified full pattern at 100 BPM.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Software timing certification, automatic strum counting, drift measurement or mastery of all syncopated sixteenth patterns.
